title: Evidence for Chapter 34: Keynes's How to Pay for the War (1940), the British budget of 1941, war economies compared, Lerner (1943), Kalecki (1943) and Domar (1944), the Keynes and White plans (1943), the Bretton Woods conference (1944) and the American hearings of 1945
source: Keynes, How to Pay for the War (London: Macmillan, 1940), the Digital Library of India's copy on the Internet Archive and its metadata; House of Commons Hansard, 7 April 1941 (Sir Kingsley Wood's Budget speech); House of Lords Hansard, 23 May 1944 (International Monetary Fund); Lerner, 'Functional Finance and the Federal Debt' (Social Research, February 1943); Kalecki, 'Political Aspects of Full Employment' (The Political Quarterly, October-December 1943); Domar, 'The "Burden of the Debt" and the National Income' (American Economic Review, December 1944); the Federal Reserve Bulletin of June 1943 (the texts of the White and Keynes plans) and September 1944 (Goldenweiser and Bourneuf, 'Bretton Woods Agreements'); the Final Act of the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference (Cmd. 6546, 1944); the hearings of the Senate Committee on Banking and Currency on the Bretton Woods Agreements Act (June 1945); the Annual Report of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System for 1942; Historical Statistics of the United States (1975), series Y 339-342; Harrison's chapters on the economics of World War II and the Soviet Union (1998) and his entry 'War finance' (1992); the Famine Inquiry Commission's Report on Bengal (1945); the judgment of the International Military Tribunal and Nazi Conspiracy and Aggression vol. II, Shizume (2009), Ide (2003) and the Bank of Japan's chronology (cached copies of Chapter 30's sources); the authority records of the Library of Congress, the Bibliothèque nationale de France and the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek
series: Evidence rows: id, place, year, values (';' separated, in the order of the quotation), unit, source key, page or column, the source text verbatim, note
license: Quotations for criticism, scholarship and teaching, each with its source; no full original is redistributed. Keynes (1883-1946): How to Pay for the War (London: Macmillan, 1940) is in the public domain in the United Kingdom but may still be in copyright in the United States, so the chapter quotes it a sentence or less at a time; the copy used is the Digital Library of India's scan, whose record reads 'dc.rights: Copyright permitted' (row km_rights). Hansard: 'Contains Parliamentary information licensed under the Open Parliament Licence v3.0.' Lerner (1903-1982), Social Research 10(1), 1943: 'Copyright, 1943, and published quarterly by the New School for Social Research, 66 West Twelfth Street, New York, N. Y. All rights reserved. Contributions to SOCIAL RESEARCH may not be reprinted without the permission of the editors.' (row ln_copyright): short phrases only, the rest paraphrased. Kalecki (1899-1970), The Political Quarterly 14(4), 1943, and Domar (1914-1997), American Economic Review 34(4), 1944: the OCR texts of the issues print no copyright line; both are in copyright, so the chapter quotes short phrases only and paraphrases the rest. Harrison (1992, 1998): the author's preprints print no copyright notice; the published chapters are in copyright (Macmillan, 1992; Cambridge University Press, 1998): short phrases only, the rest paraphrased. The Federal Reserve Bulletin, the Annual Report of the Board of Governors, the Senate hearings of 1945 and Historical Statistics of the United States (1975) are works of the United States government and in the public domain. The Final Act of Bretton Woods as presented to Parliament (Cmd. 6546, HMSO 1944) is a Crown publication of 1944, out of Crown copyright; the Articles of Agreement are also a United States government document. The Famine Inquiry Commission's Report on Bengal (Government of India, 1945) is a government publication of 1945 whose term of protection has run out; quoted briefly. The Law Library of Congress, Military Legal Resources (Nazi Conspiracy and Aggression, vol. II, and the Opinion and Judgment): 'The Library of Congress is not aware of any copyright restrictions in the Military Legal Resources collection. Absent such restrictions, these materials are free to use and reuse.' Credit line: Law Library of Congress, Military Legal Resources. Bank of Japan (Shizume 2009; the Bank's chronology): 'The information included in the site may be copied or reproduced with the exceptions below. When copying or reproducing, the source, the Bank of Japan, should be explicitly credited.' (row bjcr). Ide (2003), IMES Discussion Paper: 'Do not reprint or reproduce without permission.' (row ide_reprint); figures and short phrases only. The authority records of the Library of Congress (id.loc.gov) are public data; those of the Bibliothèque nationale de France (data.bnf.fr) are metadata reused under the Licence Ouverte (Open License); the record of the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek (GND, through lobid.org) carries the licence http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/ (row gnd_licence). The chapter's Chinese renders the quotations; the translations are the book's.
citation: See the 'source' field; each row names its source key in the 'sources' object.
notes: Every quotation is checked word for word against the cached source text by data/fetch/verify_web_quotes.py, and every value is read from its quotation by checks/check_ch34.py; rows with an empty quotation are values or words read on a page image (sources keynes1940img, domar1944img, finalact1944, arfr1942img, famine1945img, census_y34), named as such in their notes, which give a transcription between « and ». The OCR texts keep their misreadings as printed and the notes name them: in Keynes (1940) the figures of pp. 15, 16, 23 and 28 ('16' for 15, '£160' for £150, '£226' for £225, '£1,360' for £1,350, '£600' for £500, '£^0' for £450) and 'Sa.' for 5s. on p. 32, which is why those pages are read on the images, and the running head of p. 5 ('PROBLEM 6'); in Hansard 'inedaquacy' (h41_gapdef), 'practicaly' (h41_halftax), '45s. a. week' (h41_45s) and '1⅛per' (h41_short), as printed on the Historic Hansard site; in Lerner 'goo' for 900 (ln_guess), a doubled quotation mark (ln_rejects) and stray margin characters (ln_size2, '.' and 't' in ln_even, and 'r' in ln_nations); in Kalecki the byline 'Kaveckt' (kl_byline), 'toa' (kl_lecture) and a space before a closing quotation mark (kl_confidence) or after an opening one (kl_cycle); in the Federal Reserve Bulletin '137 |' for 137 1/7 (fw_unitas), 'ha/f' for 'half' (fk_ultimate), 'unti]' (fs_65) and the byline 'GotpENWEISER', 'Auice BourNEUF', 'Diwision' (fs_byline); in the Famine Inquiry Commission's report '3*5' for 3·5 (fm_35), 'he' for 'be' (fm_unsound) and '15' for 1·5 (read on the image, fm_15); in the judgment of the Tribunal 'account7'' (imt_clearing), 'rnthlessness' (imt_poland), 'Genera1' (imt_food), 'mas' for 'was' (imt_east), 'thein' for 'them' (imt_quotas) the spacing 't o', 'a t' (imt_plunder) and hyphens for the dashes around 'Oldenburg' (imt_oldenburg). Domar's Table III prints 5.71 as the limit of the tax rate for r = 2 per cent, while its row for year 300 prints 5.66 and his formula i/(r/a + i) gives 5.66; his text rounds to 5.7 (rows dm_table3, dm_3and2). Indirect testimony: Flynn (Harper's Magazine, July 1942) through Lerner (ln_argued, ln_flynn); The Economist of 20 January 1940 and Sayers (1956) through Harrison (1992) (hf_three, hf_short); the estimates of Soviet war deaths (Goskomstat; Ellman and Maksudov) through Harrison (1998) (hu_goskomstat, hu_266, hu_emigration, hu_239); Göring's assurance and the plan for the occupied Soviet territories through the judgment of the Tribunal (imt_famine, imt_starved); Sauckel's statement through the judgment (imt_sauckel, copied from alternatives_facts); K. P. Chattopadhyaya's estimate of the Bengal deaths through the Famine Inquiry Commission (fm_35). Not obtained: the White Paper on the Clearing Union (Cmd. 6437, April 1943) and the statement of principles (Cmd. 6519, April 1944) themselves (the plans are quoted from the texts the Federal Reserve Bulletin printed in June 1943; Cmd. 6519 is named only in the motion of 23 May 1944); the Proceedings and Documents of the Bretton Woods conference (Department of State, 1948); Flynn's article of July 1942; Sayers (1956); The Economist of 20 January 1940; Steil, The Battle of Bretton Woods (2013), and Skidelsky's biography of Keynes.
